<h2 class="section">The hike</h2>
```

I slept in the back of the car at the trailhead because hotels in Wicklow are priced as if Wicklow is a small principality on the Cote d'Azur. Woke up to two German tourists discussing my number plate at six in the morning. Made coffee on the camping stove. Did not make conversation.

The night before I had pulled into a forestry road off the Military Road, lit a small fire, opened a Corona and listened to a podcast about geopolitics. The wind moved through the pines. I felt extremely twenty-two and extremely smug.

Lugnaquilla at 925 metres is the highest mountain outside the Reeks and the Mournes. It climbs like a very long, very boring meeting. You go up. You keep going up. The grass is tussocky. The bog is opportunistic. Nothing dramatic happens for about two hours. The Glen of Imaal route also passes through an active artillery range. There are red flags. There are signs that explain, with admirable bluntness, that you may be killed by ordnance if the flags are flying. The flags were not flying. I read every sign anyway, because being killed by ordnance is one of those things you only do once.

At the summit I broke through the cloud. Pure inversion. The sky above was that hard, polished blue you only get in winter. The rest of Wicklow, Kildare and probably most of the midlands was a soft white duvet rolling out below. The summit plateau was empty. There was a trig point. There was me. There was a sandwich.

I sat on a rock for the better part of forty minutes, did not look at my phone, did not check the time, did not feel the need to. I have decided that those forty minutes were the best forty minutes of my year, narrowly beating a deadlift PB and a particularly satisfying Excel pivot table at work.

<h2 class="section">Reflections</h2>
```

Wicklow is my home county for hiking and I am biased. It is also genuinely brilliant. Public transport will get you nowhere useful, sadly. Bring a car or a friend with a car. Wild camping along the forestry roads off the Military Road is a grey area. Be discreet. Take everything with you. Do not light a fire near the trees.

That night I drove home reflecting on the fact I was paying for a flat in Dublin while my actual bedroom was a folded down rear seat. The flat lost the comparison.
